caseno: Writ petition Nos. 425 of 1985 and 1634 of 1988 with contempt petition No. 3 of 1987
lawyer:
Md. Hannan with M. Khaled Ahmed. Advocates ------ For the Petitioners in W.P. No. 425/85 and Contempt Petition No.3/87 and for the Respondents in W.P. No. 1634/88 

Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed with Mirza Hossain Haider and S.M. Moonir, Advocates ------ For the Petitioners in W.P. No. 1634/88 for the Respondents in W.P. No. 425/85 and for the respondent in Contempt Petition No. 3/87. 

Fakhrul Islam, A.A.G. with Md. Delwar Hossain. A.A.G ------ For the Respondent No. 3 in W.P. No. 425/85 and Contempt Petition No. 3/87

Syed Ashfaque Hossain & others  ------ Petitioners in W.P. No. 425 of 1985
Syed Mohsen Ali &others ------ Petitioners in W.P. No. 1634 of 1988
Vs. 
Bangladesh, represented by Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms and others ------ Respondents in W.P. No. 425 of 1985
Board of Land Administration and others ------ Respondents in W.P. No. 1634 of 1988
Syed Ashfaque Hossain and others ------ Petitioners in Contempt Petition No.3 of 1987
Deputy Commissioner, Moulvibazar and another ------ Contemned in Contempt Petition No. 3 of 1987
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal, J: These two Rules Nisi and the contempt petition have been heard together and will be disposed of by this common judgment as they arise out of the same transaction and involve common questions of fact and law. 

2. In Writ Petition No. 425 of 1985 the petitioner obtained the Rule Nisi challenging two Memos, namely, a Memo dated 24.4.85 (Annexure M) and a Memo dated 26.10.85 (Annexure N 1) both is- sued by the respondent No.2, Deputy Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms. 

3. The petitioners' case is that they had their ancestral home on 2.65 acres out of a total of 5.80 acres of Khatian No. 1358 of mouzaMoulvi Bazar Town which comprises several houses, tank, graveyard, gardens etc. wherein the petitioners have been living for generations now. The respondent No.4 Syed Mohsin Ali, his six brothers, two sisters and mother mutated their names in respect of the entire land of 5.80 acres of the above khatian No. 1358 on the basis of a registered Kabala No. 5879 executed and registered on 31.10.55 by one Keramat Ali in favour of Syed Ashraf Ali, deceased father of the said respondent No.4. The said Keramat Ali auction purchased the entire land of 5.80 acres of the said khatian No. 1358 on 25.9.54 for arrears of rent. The auction purchaser Keramat Ali however sold only 3.15 acres of the khatian land out of 5.80 acres to late Syed Ashraf Ali, father of the respondent No.4. The balance 2.65 acres of ancestral homestead continued to remain in the possession of the petitioners and their predecessors. The predecessors of the petitioners obtained a registered Muktipatra dated 8.5.79 from one of the sons of auction purchaser Keramat Ali, namely HabiburRahman. Thereafter the predecessors of the petitioners by executing and registering three separate deeds of gift, all dated 5.11.78, transferred their right, title and interest in the case land to the petitioners and delivered physical possession thereof to them. The petitioners thereafter instituted Mutation Case Nos. 91, 92 and 93 of 1979 be- fore the Circle Officer (Revenue), Moulvibazar. After compliance of necessary formalities all the three mutation cases were allowed vide order dated 13.11.79. The respondent No.4 Syed Mohsin Ali and his 5 brothers filed an objection petition before the Circle Officer (Revenue), Moulvi Bazar whereupon Miscellaneous Case No. 38 of 1979 was started. The par- ties were notified. After hearing the parties the Circle Officer forwarded the case record to the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Sylhet for necessary action with a detailed report as he found the case to be complicated. Then the respondent No.4 preferred an appeal before the Additional Deputy Com- missioner (Revenue), Sylhet under section 147 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, shortly the Act, against the Order dated 13.11.79 passed by the Circle Officer (Revenue), Moulvi Bazar whereupon Mutation Appeal Case No. 24 of 1979- 80 was started and the petitioners were notified. By his order dated 10.9.80 the Additional Deputy Com- missioner, Sylhet after hearing the parties rejected the appeal of the respondent No.4 and upheld the or- der dated 13.1l.79 passed by the Circle Officer (Revenue), Moulvibazar in Mutation Case Nos. 91, 92 and 93 of 1979. Against the aforesaid order of the Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Sylhet the respondent No.4 preferred an appeal before the Com- missioner, Chittagong Division being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 223 of 1980 under section 147 of the Act which was heard and disposed of by the Additional Commissioner, Chittagong Division by his order dated 15.12.82 dismissing the same and con-firming the order dated 10.9.80 passed by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Sylhet. 

4. In the meanwhile the Board of Land Administration Act, 1980 (Act No. XIII of 1981), shortly the Board Act, came into force on 30th June, 1981 whereby a Board of Land Administration was constituted with the authority to dispose of all statutory appeals vide memo No. lOM-13/82/1224-Estt. dated 3.9.82 (Annexure I). The respondent No.4 being aggrieved by the order dated 15.12.82 passed by the Additional Commissioner Chittagong Division preferred an appeal before the Board of Land Administration. The appeal was admitted, reports were called for from the Additional Commissioner, Chittagong Division and the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Sylhet. Upon perusal of the reports and hearing the parties the Board of Land Administration in Appeal Case No. 43 of 1983 by order dated 1l.l.84 contained in memo No. VI-43/ 83/92-Appeal dated 24.l.84 (Annexure K) rejected the appeal. Under section 4 of the Board Act a right of review within 60 days of the order has been provided for but the respondent No. 4 did not prefer any application for review. Instead, he preferred an incompetent appeal before the Ministry of Land Ad- ministration and Land Reforms which was admitted by the Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms, respondent No.1, on 13.1l.84 and records were called for. No notice however was served on the petitioners. In the light of orders of the Board of Land Administration (Annexure K) the petitioners went to Tahsil Office, Moulvi Bazar for payment of rent for 1392 B.S. in the last week of May, 1985 when to their surprise they came to know that the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms has since reversed the order of the Board of Land Administration exercising appellate powers under section 147 of the Act in a mutation proceeding under section 143 of the Act, allowing the objection of the respondent No.4. The petitioner No.1 came to know definitely about the aforesaid order on 2.6.85 when he came to Dhaka. A true copy of the said order was annexed as Annexure M which is the first impugned order. 

5. On 6.6.85 the petitioners filed an application before the respondent No. 1 for setting aside the ex parte impugned order Annexure M on review on grounds, inter alia, of want of jurisdiction and palpable illegality. But by memo No. VUI-604/85/1054/ 1(2) dated 26.10.85 the respondent No.1 rejected the review application, which is Annexure N1, the second impugned order. 

6. In this Writ Petition the only ground urged upon by Mr. Md. Hannan, learned Advocate for the petitioners, is that the Government had no power and jurisdiction of entertaining either any appeal or revision from the final order of the Board of Land Ad- ministration and therefore both the impugned orders Annexures M and Nl are without jurisdiction. We shall revert to the submission later on. 

7. An affidavit-in-opposition has been filed on behalf of the respondent No.4. 

8. It is stated therein that the aforesaid 5.80 acres of land of the aforesaid khatian originally be-longed to Syed Ashraf Ali, the father of respondent No.4, and Syed Ashraf Ali gifted the same to his wife SyedaAktarunnessaKhanam in lieu of her dower. The said property was sold in auction for arrears of rent and was purchased by Keramat Ali when Syed Ashraf Ali and his wife were living in Calcutta. Coming to know of the auction sale Syed Ashraf Ali obtained a kabala in his own name for valuable consideration from the said auction purchaser Keramat Ali in respect of the whole of the auction sold property, namely 5.80 acres, by kabala No. 5879 dated 31.10.55. But unfortunately the deed writer through bonafide mistake wrote 3.15 acres in place of the whole of the auction sold property, namely 5.80 acres. The recipient of the said kabala, Syed Ashraf Ali, was not aware of the said mistake in the deed as he remained in possession of the whole of 5.80 acres all along, including the period from the date of auction upto the date of the aforesaid kabala. 

9. During the rent roll operations in 1958 the entire 5.80 acres of land was wrongly recorded in the names of Syed Ashraf Ali and his brother Syed Ankar Ali, the latter having no title to or interest in the aforesaid property. In 1964 Syed Ashraf Ali allowed his nephews, namely, Syed Abdul Mannan, Syed Mozammel Ali and Syed SalehMasud to live in a portion of the aforesaid property having structures thereon, as his licencees. In 1965 Syed Ashraf Ali corrected the khatian by filing Case No. 331 of 1965 before the Circle Officer (Revenue), Moulvi Bazar by striking out of the name of his brother Syed Ankar Ali from the khatian. It is therefore absolutely incorrect that the balance 2.65 acres of ancestral home- stead continued to remain in possessive of the petitioners and their predecessors. Three nephews of Syed Ashraf Ali were only in possession of a part of the property in question. Syed Ashraf Ali died in 1970. Thereafter the heirs of Syed Ashraf Ali, namely, the respondent No.4 and his brothers and sisters requested the said licencees to surrender possession of the structures to them. At this stage they became hostile and instead of complying with the request they approached one of the sons of auction purchaser Keramat Ali, namely HabiburRahman, and obtained a so-called Muktipatrafrom him in respect of 2.65 acres out of the khatian taking advantage of mistake in respect of area in Syed Ashraf Ali's kahala dated 31.10.55 The said Muktipatra dated 8.5.79 was obtained in the names of the three licencees of Syed Ashraf Ali and another, namely Syed Abdun Noor. The Muktipatra is collusive and fraudulent. Later, Syed Abdun Noor purported to gift .64 acres of land in favour of his brother's son, namely petitioner No. 1, on 26.10.79. Syed Abdul Mannan purported to gift .65 acre on the same day to his wife who is the petitioner No. 2. Syed SalehMasud purported to gift .65 acres of land on the same day to his wife, petitioner No.3. The said donors being mere licencees and having no title to the land in question, the petitioners got no title to or interest in the lands purported to have been gifted to them. It has also been stated that after completing the aforesaid collusive and fraudulent transactions the petitioners applied to the Circle Officer (Revenue), Moulvi Bazar for mutation of their names whereupon their names were mutated in respect of 1.95 acres by an ex parte order dated 13.11.79. No notice of the aforesaid mutation ease was either issued or served upon the respondent No.4 and the order of mutation was passed in spite of objection raised by the Tahsildar which will appear from the records of the Mutation Case Nos. 91, 92 and 93 of 1979. Thereafter the respondent No.4 has more or less accepted the petitioners' description of the progress of the case from the stage of the Circle Officer (Revenue), Moulvi Bazar upto the Board of Land Administration. The said respondent however justifies his appeal before the Ministry of Land Administration on the ground that the law does not oust the Government's authority to decide a matter in respect of which the Board of Land Administration exercises appellate power.

10. However to protect his interest in the matter the respondent No.4 along with his other brothers instituted Writ Petition No. 1634 of 1988 against the petitioners as respondents and against the Government and its functionaries and obtained a Rule Nisi on 13.11.88 calling into question the or- der of the Chairman of the Board of Land Administration dated 11.1.84 passed in Appeal Case No. 43 of 1983 and which is Annexure D(2), i.e. the impugned order, in Writ Petition No. 1634 of 1988. The respondent No.4 claims that if the Rule is made absolute in Writ Petition No. 425 of 1985, then his case against the final order of the Board of Land Ad- ministration should be considered in Writ Petition No. 1634 of 1988. 

11. The averments made by the petitioners in Writ Petition No. 1634 of 1988 are the same as the averments of respondent No.4 in the affidavit-in- opposition filed in Writ Petition No. 425 of 1985. The petitioners of Writ Petition No. 425 of 1985 are respondent Nos. 4-6 in Writ Petition No. 1634 of 1988. Only respondent No.5 has filed an affidavit- in-opposition therein. The averments contained therein are almost the same as the averments contained in Writ Petition No. 425 of 1985. 

12. We shall now dispose of the petitioners' only contention in Writ Petition No. 425 of 1985, namely, that after Board of Land Administration dis- poses of an appeal under section 147 of the Act no other appeal or revision lies before the Government and therefore both the impugned orders Annexure M and N1 have been passed without jurisdiction. 

13. Section 147 of the Act, as amended up-to- date, is as follows :-"147, Appeals. Subject to any special pro- visions for appeal made in this Part or in any rules made under this Act, an appeal shall lie from every original or appellate order made un- der any of the provisions of this Part by a Revenue-officer as follows, namely :- (a) to the Collector, when the order is made by a Revenue-officer subordinate to the Collector; (b) to the Commissioner of the division, when the order is made by the Collector of a district within the division; and (c) to the Board of Land Administration, when the order is made by the Commissioner of a division". 

It may be stated that formerly appeal lay to the Government against an order made by the Commissioner of a Division but by the Laws (Amendment) Ordinance, 1982 (Ordinance No. XLI of 1982) in place of the word 'Government' the words 'Board of Land Administration' were substituted. 

14. In this connection the provisions of the Board Act may be considered. Section 3 provides that as soon may be after the commencement of this Act, the Government shall constitute a Board to be called the Board of Land Administration. It shall consist of a Chairman and not more than two other members to be appointed by the Government. The Board shall 'exercise such powers and perform such functions as may be entrusted to it by the Government or under any law. The petitioners in Writ Petition No, 4 1985 have annexed Annexure I, namely an order of the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Re- forms No. 1O-13/82/1224-Estt. dated 3.9.82 in which it has been provided under the provisions of sub-section (3) of Section 3 of the Board Act that the Board will decide all statutory appeals and revisions and perform other functions as may be provided by law. Section 4 of the Board Act however provides that within 60 days from the date of any order of the Board, an aggrieved person may apply to the Board for a review of the same. 

15." Mr. Md. Hannan submits that the respondent No.4 could have applied to the Board for a re- view of the Board's order (Annexure K) within 60 days of the same but he did not do it. He filed an appeal to the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms. There is no provision for such appeal. The Ministry was coram non juice in the matter. 

16. In this connection it may be mentioned that section 149 of the Act deals with revisions. Sub-section (3) of section 149 originally provided that the Government may, of its own motion, within six months of the date of any order passed under this Part by the Commissioner of a division or on an application made in that behalf within six months of the date of such order, revise such order. But by the Laws (Amendment) Ordinance, 1982 (Ordinance No. XLI of 1982), for the word "Government", the words "Board of Land Administration" were substituted. As such even the power of revision was parted with by the Government and the provisional power was entrusted to the Board not by any executive order but by a statutory amendment. 

17. Similarly under sub-section (4) of section 149 of the Act the Government had the power to or- der at any time the correction of any entry in a record-of-rights provided that no appeal under this section had been preferred against such order. By the said Ordinance No. XLI of 1982 in place of the word "Government", the words "Board of Land Administration" have been substituted in sub-section (4) as well. 

18. Me. Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate for the respondent No.4 in WritPetition No. 425 of 1985, faced with this difficulty, feebly argued that in spite of the statutory amendment relegating to the Board of Land Administrationthe powers of hearing and disposal of appeals and revisions, the Government, as the overall supervisory authority of all revenue officers and revenue administration, possesses the inherent jurisdiction to revise and modify any order passed by the Board of LandAdministration. Therefore, even if the appeal of the respondent NO.4 to the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms was incompetent, it can be treated as a provisional application and the Government should be deemed to have exercised its inherent provisional power in disposing of the same. 

19. Apart from the fact that we do not find any final provisional power within the four comers of the Act itself, we consider it to be a hazardous leap into the dark to invest the Government with an imaginary power by way of a bonus. The Government itself possessed the full powers of an appellate and provisional body. It handed over those powers to the Board by a statutory amendment, without reserving any residuary power to itself to act as an authority of last resort. In the absence of any legislative intention investing the Government with the authority of a residuary power we arc frankly unable to see how the Government could have exercised the appellate or re- visional power in respect of the application of the respondent No.4. The order of the Board of Land Administration, Annexure K in Writ Petition No. 425 of 1985, appears to have drawn the certain of finality in the proceedings and the matter, it appears, cannot be dragged any further, except by way of a challenge under Article 102 of the Constitution. 

20. In that view of the matter we are of the opinion that the Rule Nisi in Writ Petition No. 425 of 1985 ought to be made absolute. 

21. With regard to Writ Petition No. 1634 of 1988 it is the contention of Mr. Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate for the petitioners, that the Board of Land Administration by the impugned order; Annexure D(2), has addressed itself to   a wrong question which has gone into the root of its jurisdiction. He submits that Mutation Case Nos. 91,92 and 93 of 1979 are themselves without jurisdiction, not maintainable under section 143 of the Act and the Board has failed to address itself on this question. He has cited no decision in support of his argument. Section 143 of the Act, as amended up-to-date, is as follows:-	

143. Maintenance of the Record-of-rights. The Collector shall maintain up-to-date, in the prescribed manner, the record-of-rights prepared or revised under Part IV of under this Part by correcting clerical mistakes and by incorporating therein the changes on account of - 
(a) the mutation of names as a result of transfer or inheritance.
(b) the subdivision, amalgamation or consolidation of holdings; 
(c) the new settlement of'lands or of holdings purchased by the Government ; and 
(d) the abatement of rent on account of abandonment or diluvia or acquisition of land." 

22. Indeed we find that the petitioners have all throughout agitated that the alleged transfer by the predecessors of respondent Nos. 4-6 having not been effected by a recorded tenant, proceedings under section 143 are entirely misconceived. 111is is what the petitioners specifically argued before the Circle Officer (Revenue), Moulvi Bazar (vide Order dated 28.11.79 in Miscellaneous Case No. 38 of 1979 Annexure F of Writ Petition No. 425 of 1985), in their Memo of Appeal before the Commissioner, Chittagong Division (ground Nos. 2 and 3 of Annexure H in Writ Petition No. 425 of 1985) and also before the Board of Land Administration (ground No. IV of the appeal petition Annexure J in Writ Petition No. 425 of 1985) 

23. The Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Sylhet, the Additional Commissioner, Chittagong and the Board of Land Administration in their respective orders came to a finding that Keramat Ali auction purchased the entire 5.80 acres of case khatian. Syed Ashraf Ali purchased only 3.15 acres from him. After Syed Ashraf Ali's death, names of his heirs were mutated, but they are entitled to have their land mutated to the extent of purchase by their predecessor-in-interest. It is for them to establish in a Court of law that Syed Ashraf Ali actually purchased 5.80 acres. The respondent Nos. 4-6 and their predecessors were and are in possession of the remaining portion. So they are entitled to mutate their names. 

24. The question is, is such mutation permit- ted under section 143 of the Act? Chapter IV of the Act contains an elaborate procedure for preparing the record-of-rights and also for hearing objections from parties concerned. S.A. khatian No. 1358 was pre- pared in the joint names of Syed Ashraf Ali and his brother Syed Ankar Ali during the rent roll operations in 1958. No objections were filed by the predecessors of the respondent Nos. 4-6. Thekhatian was corrected in 1965 by Syed Ashraf Ali and thereafter it stood in his sole name. After his death in 1970, his heirs and successors mutated their names in Mutation Case No. 75 of 1973-74. No objections were filed at that time. 

25. Section 143 of the Act is attracted only when a clerical mistake is to be corrected or, inter alia, the mutation of names as a result of transfer or inheritance is necessary. It is not attracted when the record-of-rights is to be corrected after a finding to be given as to the title of the holders or the challengers. The examination of title deeds for purposes of determination title or the holder of record of rights is not permitted under section 143. The word "transfer" referred to in clause (a) of section 143 is limited to transfer by the recorded tenant, not by other persons. The respondent Nos. 4-6 applied for mutation not because the recorded tenant transferred the lands to them, but because some persons, unconnected with record of rights, transferred the lands. Clause (a) of Section 143 is not attracted under these circumstances. 
26. By E.P. Ordinance No. VIII of 1965 section 143A was inserted into the Act which reads as follows:- "(1) Any person aggrieved by an entry or omission of entry in the record-or-rights pre- pared or revised and finally published under Chapter IV may, notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in this Act, file an application along with necessary requisites for the purpose of correcting mistakes in such record-of-rights in the Civil Court which could have jurisdiction to entertain a suit for possession of the land to which such entry relates or in respect of which such omission was made." 

27. It is not- necessary to quote the other pro- visions of section 143A. 

28. Section 143A was omitted by Ordinance No. LXIV of 1975 

29. The respondent Nos. 4-6 and their predecessors, claiming as they do the disputed property as their ancestral property from time immemorial, had a remedy from 1965-1975 to file an application in the Civil Court for the purpose of correcting mistakes in the record-of-rights. The question could have been decided on the basis of possession only. This they failed to do. Now that Syed Ashraf Ali is the recorded tenant and his heirs and successors have also been substituted after his death, transferees of persons unconnected with the record of rights do not have any locus standi under section 143 of the Act to maintain an application for mutation. Such transferees have now to take recourse to Civil Court for establishment of their predecessors' right, title, interest and possession and it is only when they do so establish that the question of mutation will arise. 

30. It is well-established that a determination that is erroneous in law can be set aside if the error goes to jurisdiction or if the error is apparent on the face of the record. We find that the Board of Land Ad- ministration has misdirected itself as to the question of law involved in this case and has decided matters which are not within its jurisdiction to decide under scction143. We arc of the opinion that under such circumstances the decision of the Board of Land Administration is liable to interference by this Court. 

31. At one time section 143 of the Act stood as follows:- "143. The Collector shall maintain up-to-date, in prescribed manner, the record-of-rights prepared or revised under Part IV under this Part by correcting bonafide mistakes and by incorporating therein the changes on account of- 
(a) the mutation of names as a result of transfer or inheritance; 
(b) the subdivision, amalgamation or consolidation of holdings; 
(c) the new settlement of land or holdings purchased by the Government; and 
(d) the abatement of rent on account of abandonment or diluvium or acquisition ofland." 

32. In the unreported decision of the Appellate Division in the case of Bangladesh and others-Vs- MariumKhatun and others (Civil Appeal No.8 of 1972) the facts are that the respondent who, along with others took settlement of land from Zaminders and were in in possession thereof, challenged the or- der of the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Faridpur cancelling the names of the respondent and his co-sharers from the record of rights which were recorded in the name of the then Province of East Pakistan. By four different orders from 1960 to 1963 the Revenue Settlement Officer corrected the record of rights and inserted the names of the respondent and his co-sharers in the disputed khatian. The Deputy Commissioner of Faridpur purchased some of the land in dispute from the respondent in 1964, but on 17.10.66 the respondent and his co-sharers were served with notice to show cause why the record of rights shall not be changed in favour of the Province of East Pakistan. The respondent showed cause but the Additional Deputy Com- missioner (Revenue), Faridpur cancelled the names of the respondent and his co-sharers by order dated 13.7.67 and inserted the name of the Province of East Pakistan in respect of the disputed Khatian. The case of the Province of East Pakistan was that the names of the respondent and his co-sharers were re- corded as a result of fraudulent transaction between the respondent and his co-sharers on the one hand and some of the revenue authorities on the other. 

33. The Appellate Division quoted with approval the judgment of the then Dhaka High Court in Writ Petition No. 386 of 1967 arising out of the above proceeding as follows :- 

"The scope of section 143 of the Act is, in our opinion, of a very limited nature. It authorizes the Collector to maintain up to date record of rights and to make such correction as occurred as a result of bonafide mistake committed in preparing the record of rights. It does not, in our opinion, authorise the Collector to correct the record-of-rights which affects the question of title or possession relating to disputed question of fact. Bonafide mistake, as contemplated under section 143 of the Act, in our opinion, relates to the mistake of the nature where a mistake has crept in which is not supported by the records or where there has been a mistake in recording quantum of the land which again is not supported by facts but where name of a person stands recorded and another person challenges that such entry cannot be said to have been made as a result of bonafide mistake, and that cannot be corrected by the Collector under section 143 of the Act." 

34. The Appellate Divisionwas unable to find fault with or take exception to the views so expressed. The Appellate Division held that the facts which were required to be determined prior to correcting the record-of-rights by a proceeding under Section 143 of the Act involved the examination of documents of title relating to the lands in dispute, commission of fraud, if any, and the interpretation of various sections of the Act. The summary method under section 143 cannot be strained to consider question relating to such facts. 

35. In the present case also the questions, for example, whether Syed Ashraf All purchased 5.80 acres or only 3.15 acres, whether the predecessors of respondent Nos. 4-6 were possessing the remaining 2.65 acres as ancestral land and if so under what title, whether the Muktiptara dated 8.5.79 created any title in favour of the predecessors of respondent Nos. 4-6 and other questions can be determined only after examining witnesses and documents in a full-scale title suit. None of these things can conveniently or even suitably be done by the Collector 'under the terms and provisions of aforesaid section 143, as it now stands. If "bonafide mistake" was not covered by the facts disclosed in the aforesaid Civil Appeal No. 8 of 1972, we fail to see how "clerical mistake" can be found in the present case. 36. In the Rule Nisi obtained in Writ Petition No. 1634 of 1988 the respondents have also been asked to show cause why direction should not be issued for cancellation of the Board's order and restoration of the record in the names of the petitioners to the extent of 5.80 acres. 
37. From the above we are of the opinion that the petitioners arc also entitled to get the said direction in full. 

38. In Contempt Petition No. 3 of 1987 the petitioners of Writ Petition No. 425 of 1985 have alleged that while obtaining a Rule Nisi on 13.11.85 in Writ Petition No. 425 of 1985, the petitioners obtained a stay of operation of the impugned orders Annexure M and Ni. But violating the order of stay the Deputy Commissioner of Moulvi Bazar and the respondent No. 4 mutally and in collusion with each other caused an amendment in the record-of-rights showing the respondent No. 4 as the recorded tenant. As a proof thereof the petitioners have annexed in their supplementary affidavit Annexure 6 showing that on 19.2.87, i.e., about 2 years after issuance on the Rule Nisi and stay order, the record-of-rights was corrected in favour of the respondent No. 4 in pursuance of the impugned order Annexure M passed by the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Re-forms.

 39. In a counter-affidavit the respondent No. 3, the Deputy Commissioner, Moulvi Bazar has denied the allegations and has stated that he did not pass any order for the alleged correction of records. 

40. We find that the Contempt Rule was is-sued not by name upon any particular officer but by designation upon the Deputy Commissioner, Moulvi Bazar. The law of Contempt acts in persona and therefore the issuance of the Rule upon an office is of no consequence. That leaves us with the question as to whether the respondent No. 4 himself has taken any part in the correction of records after the High Court Division passed an order of stay on 13.11.85. We do not find any material in support of the allegation that the respondent No. 4 himself was responsible or was instrumental in effecting any correction.

 41. In that view of the matter we do not find any substance in this Rule.

 42. In the result the Rule Nisi in Writ Petition No. 425 of 1985 is made absolute without any order as to costs. Annexures M and Ni thereof are declared to have been passed without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect. The respondent No. 1 is directed to cancel/rescind and/ or withdraw the impugned orders. 
	
43. The Rule Nisi in Writ Petition No. 1634 of 1988 is also made absolute without any order as to costs. It is declared that the, impugned order Annexure D(2) has been passed without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect and the respondent No. 1 is directed to cancel the same and the respondent No. 3 is directed to restore the records in the names of the petitioners to the extent of 5.80 acres as it originally stood. 

44. The Rule in Contempt Petition No. 3 of 1987 is discharged. 

End.
